assumptions.text: A timeout is retried, as the description says.
assumptions.quote: fail with a 5xx or a timeout are now retried with exponential backoff

evidence.observation: The only call is requests.post with timeout=5 and there is no try/except: a timeout raises and leaves deliver() instead of being retried.

assumptions.text: The loop ends at some point.
assumptions.quote: loops until the endpoint answers with something other than a 5xx

evidence.observation: The loop is `while True` with no maximum number of attempts, and the delay has no cap.

assumptions.text: Customers' endpoints tolerate receiving the same event twice.
assumptions.quote: so customers stop losing events during their deploys
assumptions.check: Look at one delivered request (body and headers): is there an event id or idempotency key a receiver can deduplicate on?

assumptions.text: Any answer below 500 is final and must not be retried.

evidence.observation: Only status codes of 500 and above continue the loop; every lower code returns at once.

assumptions.text: deliver() runs in a background worker, not in a request path or a shared pool.
assumptions.check: git grep -n 'deliver(' -- '*.py' and read the callers: which thread or pool runs them?

attacks.quote: resp = requests.post(endpoint.url, json=payload, timeout=5) if resp.status_code < 500:
attacks.attack: A timeout raises requests.Timeout and nothing catches it: the first slow endpoint aborts the delivery and the event is lost, although the description promises that timeouts are retried.
attacks.check: Point deliver() at a server that sleeps 10 seconds and check that Timeout reaches the caller.

attacks.attack: An endpoint that always answers 503 keeps its delivery in the loop for ever, and the delay doubles without a cap: by the 21st failure one sleep lasts about 12 days, so nothing is retried in any useful time.
attacks.check: Run deliver() against a server that always answers 503 with time.sleep patched, and count the attempts and the delays.

attacks.attack: Whoever can register a webhook URL can point it at an endpoint that always answers 503: every event for that customer holds a worker for ever, so one tenant starves the deliveries of all the others.
attacks.check: Register a test endpoint that always answers 503, send 50 events and watch worker utilisation.

attacks.attack: Each retrying delivery blocks a worker for its whole backoff: when many customers deploy at the same time, the pool is full of sleeping deliveries and new events wait behind them.
attacks.check: Simulate 200 endpoints answering 503 for 5 minutes and measure the queue time of a healthy endpoint.

attacks.quote: so customers stop losing events during their deploys
attacks.attack: Retrying a request that timed out can deliver the same event twice, and nothing in the diff adds an event id or idempotency key; receivers that are not idempotent will process it twice.
attacks.check: Inspect a delivered payload and its headers for an event id.

attacks.attack: A 429 Too Many Requests or a 408 Request Timeout is a 4xx that means try again later, but the loop treats it as final and drops the event.
attacks.check: Run deliver() against a server that answers 429 once and then 200, and check whether the second call happens.

skipped_classes.reason: Pure code change with no schema, queue or persisted state: reverting the commit restores the old behavior.
